extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, legal scholars, and the environmental law/policy community interested in EPA greenhouse gas regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of an Institute for Policy Integrity report offering legal analysis and policy recommendations about how the EPA should regulate greenhouse gases under the Clean Air Act and how to avoid conflict with Congress and future cap-and-trade legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflict with Congress when regulating greenhouse gases
rubrics_metrics.description: If the EPA pursues traditional command-and-control regulation under the Clean Air Act, it may set itself on a collision course with Congress, which has been moving to design cap-and-trade legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report warns that EPA action that conflicts with Congressional movement toward cap-and-trade should be avoided because it creates legal and political friction; EPA should design programs mindful of ongoing legislative efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Clean Air Act flexibility wisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Clean Air Act, the EPA has a great deal of flexibility to design regulatory programs and it must use that flexibility wisely to avoid a conflict with Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices (scope, mechanisms, timing) should leverage statutory flexibility in ways that reduce the risk of legal or policy collision with prospective congressional legislation; this is a central recommendation of the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize meeting legal obligations while allowing Congress room to legislate
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s top priority should be to meet its legal obligations while giving Congress enough breathing room to legislate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As Michael Livermore argues, the agency should balance fulfilling statutory duties with restraint that permits Congress to act, thereby applying 'smart regulation' that pressures but does not foreclose legislative solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mandatory control approaches that create large transition costs
rubrics_metrics.description: If the EPA adopts mandatory control regulation and Congress later enacts a cap-and-trade system, there will be significant and unnecessary transition costs for the American economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory designs should account for the possibility of later congressional action; avoid hard-to-reverse mandatory controls that would impose high transition costs if a different national system (e.g., cap-and-trade) is later implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation preferred for democratic legitimacy and policy longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation would provide a better democratic 'stamp' and help ensure the longevity of the policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report and authors note that while executive or administrative measures can act more quickly, statute-based solutions are preferable for democratic legitimacy and durability; this factor should weigh into decisions about regulatory ambition and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive action is a possible fallback if Congress fails to act
rubrics_metrics.description: If Congress does not act, the President could create a cap-and-trade system on his own, complete with auctions and the ability to sign an international agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not ideal, executive options exist and could be used as a last resort; regulators and policymakers should recognize the existence and implications of this fallback when assessing policy choices and political strategy.
